sentences.text: Camelotia is described as a robust, large-bodied sauropodomorph, though it is incompletely known.
The holotype femur is approximately 1 meter long, suggesting the animal was roughly 8-10 meters in length based on scaling comparisons.
The largest individuals of Camelotia borealis had an estimated length of 12 meters.
Camelotia borealis possessed many small to medium-sized, leaf-shaped teeth in its jaws.
Camelotia borealis had five digits on each hand and foot, with hands that were particularly long, narrow, and equipped with a large claw.
Camelotia borealis had forelimbs longer than its hind limbs, contrasting with more derived sauropods.
Camelotia is estimated to have reached a body length of 8-10 meters and a mass of 3.8 tonnes, making it one of the largest sauropodomorphs from the Triassic.
The genus name Camelotia is derived from the legendary castle of Camelot, sometimes located in Somerset.
The specific name C. borealis means "northern" and refers to Camelotia being the only known melanorosaurid in the Northern Hemisphere according to Galton.

The first large dinosaur remains in the Triassic of England were discovered in 1894 in the parish of Wedmore after quarrying exposed fragments that were brought to William Ayshford Sanford by Sydenham Henry Augustus Hervey.
Harry Govier Seeley published a description of the initial collection in 1898, which included two teeth, multiple hindlimb and foot bones, dorsal and caudal vertebrae, and ribs.
The type species C. borealis was first described by Galton in 1985 after reassigning remains previously identified as Avalonianus and Gresslyosaurus.
Camelotia was redescribed by Galton in 1998.
Phylogenetic analysis suggests Camelotia was close to Sauropoda and likely adopted quadrupedality, though its locomotion remains uncertain due to incomplete remains.
Associated dentition from the same beds features serrated, leaf-shaped crowns typical of herbivorous sauropodomorphs.
Camelotia belongs to the class Saurischia.
The parent group for Camelotia is Sauropodiformes.
The type species of the genus Camelotia is Camelotia borealis.
Current phylogenetic analyses generally place Camelotia in the family Melanorosauridae, a relationship noted by von Huene in 1929, closely related to Lessemsaurus and Melanorosaurus.
The lesser trochanter of the femur shows characteristics of Plateosauridae, or "Prosauropoda".
The presence of a fourth projection on the femur is a characteristic of Sauropoda.
In lateral view, the distal part of the Camelotia femur is straight, a characteristic of Sauropoda.
Recent classifications place Camelotia close to Melanorosauridae or as a basal sauropodiform just outside Sauropoda, with some analyses suggesting it might be a basal sauropod.
Camelotia lived during the latest Triassic (Rhaetian) in southwest England.
Camelotia lived approximately 209 million years ago during the Rhaetian stage of the Late Triassic in what is now Europe.
Fossils of Camelotia borealis date from 208.5 to 201.3 million years ago.
The time range for Camelotia is the Rhaetian, from 205.7 to 201.4 million years ago.
It is uncertain whether probable large sauropodomorph trackways assigned to the ichnogenus Eosauropus near Penarth were produced by Camelotia.
Peter M. Galton suggested in 1998 that theropod teeth historically assigned to Avalonianus, which were associated with the Camelotia holotype, actually represent the species Newtonsaurus cambrensis.
Paleontologists are divided on which family to assign Camelotia to; it was generally considered a prosauropod, but others include it within Melanorosauridae, a group of primitive sauropods.
It is still not clear whether Camelotia is a large Plateosaurid or a sauropod.

While the distal end of the femur in Camelotia shows a curvature typical of Sauropoda, American paleontologist Gregory S. Paul suggests it is the most basal known sauropod and thus not a Melanorosaurid.
